The White Heron: a castle whose keep has stood since 1609, through the end of the samurai and the bombing of the city around it.

Himeji lies in Harima, the old province in the southwest of what is now Hyōgo Prefecture, on the corridor that joined the capital region of Kyoto and Osaka to the rest of western Japan. The rivers of the Banshū plain made it good farmland, and the Harimanada, the sea to the south, fed it. That position is why so many castles were built in the area, and why Himeji’s was the one that mattered.[2][3]

Ikeda Terumasa, who held the castle from 1600, ringed the town as well as the castle with moats and earth banks, so that Himeji had three layers of defence: the outer town, a middle ring where the samurai lived, and the castle itself. The higher a samurai’s rank, the closer he lived to the centre; merchants and craftsmen lived just beyond the middle moat, and some districts were named for their trades, such as Zaimoku-machi, the lumber town, and Takajō-machi, the falconers’ town.

After the domains were abolished in 1871 the castle became an army base, and the samurai quarter in front of its main gate a parade ground. In 1945 American air raids destroyed the city, but the castle came through almost untouched.[3]

Himeji was once known for growing ginger and making soy sauce, and the two meet in its own way of eating oden, the simmered hotpot: here it comes with ginger soy sauce poured over it. The habit seems to have taken hold in the late 1930s and early 1940s, and more than 100 places in the city now serve it. For breakfast, Himeji’s cafés serve almond toast, bread spread thickly with a sweet almond butter.[4]

The head temple of the Kōyasan school of Shingon Buddhism, a former memorial temple of Hideyoshi’s with Japan’s largest rock garden.

Kūkai, born in 774 in Sanuki on Shikoku, went to China in 804 and studied esoteric Buddhism in Chang’an under the master Huiguo. In 816 Emperor Saga granted him the mountain, and he and his disciples cut a path, cleared the forest and began building a monastery on its high, level ground far from the capital.

The temple tells how he found it: before sailing home from China he threw a ritual implement into the air, praying to be shown where to build. In Japan a hunter with a black dog and a white dog led him across the Kinokawa River into the mountains, a goddess of the mountain promised her help, and he found the implement caught in a pine tree on a quiet plateau.[2][3]

Kōyasan has no single temple in the usual sense: the mountain as a whole is the temple, and its main hall is the Kondō of the Danjō Garan, where nearly all the great ceremonies are held. The Garan is the first place Kūkai built, laid out to express the world of the Womb Realm mandala; its Konpon Daitō, begun in 816 and finished in 887, is believed to be Japan’s first square two-storey pagoda. Around it, 117 temples stand along the streets.
Until 1872 women were not allowed on the mountain at all, and prayed instead at halls by each of its entrances; one of those halls survives.[3][6]

About half of the mountain’s 117 temples take in guests, and staying in one is how most visitors meet Kōyasan’s daily life. Guests are asked to dress modestly at the sacred sites, to change out of the temple’s yukata before the morning service, and to keep to the places where photography is allowed. At Kongōbu-ji, visitors are given tea and a rice cracker in its great hall of 169 tatami mats.[3][1]

The temples that take guests serve shōjin ryōri, the Buddhist cooking made only from vegetables and wild plants, with nothing from animals. Kōyasan’s own specialities are kōya-dōfu, freeze-dried tofu, and goma-dōfu, a smooth tofu made with sesame; both turn up in the restaurants along the road between Okunoin and the Danjō Garan as well.[4]

Emperor Kanmu ordered the capital moved here in 794 and had it laid out on the model of Chinese capitals such as Chang’an and Luoyang: an 84-metre avenue, Suzaku-ōji, ran north to south, with streets in a symmetrical grid on either side.

Its name, Heian-kyō, means capital of peace and tranquillity. It rarely had either. The Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 was fought in its streets and opened a century of civil war; Fushimi Inari’s buildings were among those burned.[1][5]
Snow at the Gion Shrine, from the series Famous Places in Kyoto, Utagawa Hiroshige (Japanese, 1797–1858), mid-1830s. Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access, CC0 1.0.
Shoguns set up governments in Kamakura and later in Edo, but the imperial court stayed in Kyoto, and much of the country’s political and cultural life with it, until 1869.[1][6]

The World Heritage listing covers 17 properties: 13 Buddhist temples, three Shinto shrines and Nijō Castle, spread across Kyoto, Uji and Ōtsu. Only buildings and gardens with Japan’s highest protection were eligible.
Kiyomizu-dera is one of them. Fushimi Inari Taisha and Nishiki Market are not, which says more about the rules of the listing than about either place.[3]

Kyoto lies in a basin with mountains on three sides, and about three quarters of the city’s area, which runs a long way north to south, is forest. The ring of hills shapes everything from the views to the weather: summers are hot, with an average high of 33.7°C in August, and January nights fall close to freezing.
When the capital moved to Tokyo in 1869 the city answered with public works, the so-called Kyoto Policy: the Lake Biwa Canal, a public water supply and the city’s first streetcars.[7][2]

Kyoto has been wrecked by war more than once, and each time, the city says, it was its own townspeople, the machishū, who brought it back. Losing the capital in 1869 halved its population of 400,000. In the Second World War it suffered no major air raids, though many houses were pulled down and people and resources left the city.

Its mountains also left little room for large factories. Kyoto became instead a city of universities and of technology companies, many of them founded here since the Meiji era, some by combining old crafts such as ceramics with new industry.[7][8]

The city holds more than 2,000 shrines and temples and 14 of the components of its World Heritage listing. About a fifth of Japan’s National Treasures and some 15% of its Important Cultural Properties are in Kyoto.

The city describes itself as the place where much of what is now called Japanese culture took shape, out of the meeting of the court’s refinement and the Zen-influenced culture of the samurai: the tea ceremony, flower arrangement and Japanese cuisine among them. Since 1978 it has called itself a city open to the free exchange of world culture, and the national Agency for Cultural Affairs is moving its headquarters here.[7][9]

Kyoto eats from its own vegetables, from freshwater fish of Lake Biwa and from a handful of sea fish prized here, among them hamo, the pike conger, and guji, the tilefish, along with yuba made from soy milk skin and fu, cakes of wheat gluten. The same ingredients go into the city’s formal restaurant cooking and into obanzai, the everyday home cooking of Kyoto households.
Nishiki Market, called Kyoto’s kitchen, is where both kinds of cooking shop, and the crush there at the end of the year, as people buy for the New Year, is itself a Kyoto tradition.[10][9]

People in Kyoto have long kept the seasons in their daily lives, in food, customs and the year’s events. In the heat of summer, households splash water on the street in front of their doors to cool it, a custom called uchimizu, and the traditional townhouses, Kyō-machiya, are built to let air through. The Gion, Aoi and Jidai festivals are the city’s three great festivals; at the end of the Bon season, the Gozan Okuribi bonfires on the surrounding mountains send the spirits of the ancestors back, and small Jizōbon festivals bind each neighbourhood together.
It is also a young city. Kyoto has 36 universities and colleges and about 150,000 students, a tenth of everyone who lives here.[7][8]

Nara, then called Heijō-kyō, was founded as the capital in 710 and laid out on a grid after the capital of China. It stayed the capital until the court moved to Kyoto in 794, so the city is the older layer beneath much of what Kyoto later became. Envoys sent again and again to China brought back its learning, and the eighth-century culture that grew from it, called Tenpyō, produced Buddhist art, sculpture and crafts that later Japanese culture built on.
The state built great temples here to pray for the peace of the country, Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji among them, and they were centres of learning as much as of worship.[1]

The site of the imperial palace is now a wide open field in the west of the city, with its audience hall, its Suzaku Gate, where foreign envoys were first received, and an east garden rebuilt from excavation and old records. In the east, the city climbs into Nara Park and the wooded hills of Kasuga and Wakakusa, where Kasuga Taisha stands in its primeval forest.[4][1]

Beside the park, Naramachi was part of the old capital, then a religious centre and later the town’s market quarter. Its townhouses and temples date from the Edo period to the years after the Second World War. Red cloth monkeys hang under the eaves: migawarizaru, charms that take misfortune in a person’s place, traditionally one for each member of the household.

Its temple, Gangō-ji, descends from Asuka-dera, Japan’s oldest Buddhist temple, which was moved here with the capital; some of its roof tiles are older than the move. Mochiidono, the shopping street leading into the district, is said to be the oldest in Japan still trading.[5]

Nara’s old breakfast was cha-gayu, rice cooked in roasted tea and eaten with pickles; narazuke, vegetables soaked in sake lees, has been made for more than 1,300 years. Nara is inland, far from the sea, and fish was once precious, so for kaki-no-ha-zushi mackerel or salmon is salted, laid on vinegared rice and wrapped in persimmon leaves to keep it from drying out. Manjū, the bean-filled buns found all over Japan, are said to have been first made here in the fourteenth century.[6]

For more than twelve centuries the deer of Nara have been protected as messengers of the god of Kasuga, and they are as much a part of the city as its temples. They are counted every July; in 2026 there were 1,687, the most in the preservation foundation’s records.[7][3]

Osaka stands where rivers flowing down to Osaka Bay meet the busy Seto Inland Sea. In the fifth century its port, Naniwazu, believed to have stood in what is now Chūō ward, was Japan’s gateway to Korea and China, and the people who came through it brought new crafts, metalworking, ceramics and, before long, Buddhism.
In 645 Emperor Kōtoku moved the capital here. The ruins of his Naniwa Palace, considered the oldest imperial palace in Japan, are now a park in the city.[2]

In 1496 the priest Rennyo began building a temple and monks’ lodging on the Uemachi Plateau, the high ground of the city, and Ishiyama Hongan-ji grew into a fortress. Oda Nobunaga besieged it for more than ten years until most of it burned. His successor, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, built Osaka Castle on the site in 1583; the moats and widened rivers he dug turned the town into a port and transport hub linked to the sea.[2][3]

Once the Tokugawa had moved the seat of power to Edo, Osaka rebuilt itself from the ashes as a city of trade. Rice and food from all over the country were bought and sold here and shipped on to the rest of Japan, and Osaka became known as the kitchen of the nation.

An old saying sets it against Kyoto: Kyoto spends its money on clothes, Osaka on eating. The bay was so rich in fish that it was nicknamed Naniwa, the fish garden; the knives came from nearby Sakai and the sake from Ikeda, Itami and Nada; and merchants who did business over meals pushed the cooks to refine their craft. The city’s word for all this is kuidaore, which its tourism bureau renders as eating to your heart’s content.[2][4]

Its merchants’ money built a culture of its own, aimed at ordinary townspeople: the puppet theatre jōruri, the forerunner of Bunraku, and Osaka’s own kabuki. The city also had schools whose scholars shaped the country; Tekijuku, founded for Western science and medicine, was one of them.
Dōtonbori, the canal street that grew up around its theatres, is still where the city goes out to eat and be entertained.[2][5]

/japan/kansai/himeji/himeji-castle/: The White Heron: a castle whose keep has stood since 1609, through the end of the samurai and the bombing of the city around it.

Himeji’s keep has stood since 1609, through the end of the samurai, an army garrison and the firebombing of its city. Its walls, gates, galleries and the town plan around it show how a castle of that age actually worked.
Keep dismantled and rebuilt, 1956-1964[1]

A fortress at Himeji is first recorded in 1561, held by the Kuroda clan. Toyotomi Hideyoshi made it his base for taking the west of Honshu and built a three-storey keep there. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu gave the castle and the province of Harima to his son-in-law Ikeda Terumasa, who between 1601 and 1609 built a new, larger keep. Its white plastered walls gave the castle its name, the White Heron.

Under the Tokugawa the lords of Himeji changed more often than almost anywhere else. The castle guarded the route west, so it was never left to a child: when a lord died without an adult heir, his family was moved elsewhere at once.[1]

After the end of the domains the castle became a base for the army’s 10th Regiment, and neglect and lack of money for repairs wore the old buildings down. In 1945 the keep was covered with camouflage, and when American bombers destroyed the city of Himeji the castle survived almost unharmed; local stories tell of a firebomb that landed inside without exploding.

Between 1956 and 1964 the entire keep was dismantled, repaired and put back together. Finding timbers big enough was the hardest part: one trunk meant to replace a main pillar broke while it was being brought from the Kiso mountains.[1]

The head temple of the Kōyasan school of Shingon Buddhism, a former memorial temple of Hideyoshi’s with Japan’s largest rock garden.

Kongōbu-ji is where the mountain is run from. Its buildings carry the history of how Kōyasan survived the age of the warlords, and its rooms the story of one of them, Hideyoshi’s nephew, who died here.
Since 1869, when two temples were merged[1]

In the late sixteenth century Toyotomi Hideyoshi prepared to attack Kōyasan, and the monk Ōgo, known as Mokujiki, negotiated its survival. Hideyoshi let him build a temple on this site, and in 1593 he added a second, Seigan-ji, in memory of his mother. The two stood side by side until 1869, when they were merged and renamed Kongōbu-ji. Its lanterns still carry two crests: on the right that of the shrine whose gods guard the mountain, on the left the paulownia of the Toyotomi.
In the Willow Room, Hideyoshi’s nephew and heir Toyotomi Hidetsugu took his own life in 1595.[1]

The main hall was rebuilt in 1863 after several fires. Its roof is laid in cypress bark fixed with bamboo nails, and on top of it stand wooden barrels that collected rainwater, so that monks could climb up and wet the roof against flying sparks.

The Banryūtei rock garden, made in 1984 for the 1,150th anniversary of Kūkai’s entry into eternal meditation, covers 2,340 square metres. Its 140 stones, granite from Shikoku where Kūkai was born, form a pair of dragons rising from a sea of clouds of white sand from Kyoto.[1]

/japan/kansai/koyasan/okunoin/: The resting place of Kōbō Daishi, approached through a forest of cedars and graves, where lanterns have been kept burning for a thousand years.
For Shingon Buddhists, Kōbō Daishi did not die but entered eternal meditation here, and the forest of graves and memorials that lines the way to his mausoleum is people wanting to be near him.
Enlarged to its present size in 1023 by Fujiwara no Michinaga[2]

Kūkai died on 21 March 835, at the age of 62, sitting in meditation. On the fiftieth day, as he had asked, his disciples placed his body in a grotto at Okunoin. The mausoleum there, the Gobyō, is one of the centres of faith on the mountain, the place where Kōbō Daishi is said to have entered the next world, and an inscription at the great gate of Kōyasan says he appears every morning to make his rounds.[1][2]

The Hall of Lanterns in front of the mausoleum was built by Kūkai’s successor Shinzen and enlarged to its present size by the statesman Fujiwara no Michinaga in 1023. Some of its lanterns have been kept alight continuously: one given by Emperor Shirakawa, and one offered by a poor woman who cut off and sold her hair to pay for it. Sutras are chanted there six times a day, and on 13 August and from 1 to 3 October the hall reopens at night for lantern festivals.[2]

Emperors kept villas here for the view, and Japan’s first Zen temple stood on the same ground. Tenryū-ji, founded on it in 1339, was ranked first among Kyoto’s Zen temples, and the river, bridge and hills around it are still the city’s favourite landscape.
First of Kyoto’s Five Mountains, the leading Zen temples[1]
Tenryū-ji, with the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto[2]

Arashiyama lies at the foot of the mountains on Kyoto’s western edge. South of Tenryū-ji the Katsura River comes out of the rugged Hozu Gorge and passes under Togetsu-kyō, the long bridge; Kameyama Park climbs the hills to the west. All of it was once the temple’s land.

The ground has an older Zen history still. In the ninth century Empress Tachibana no Kachiko founded Danrin-ji here, the first Zen temple in Japan. When it fell into ruin, the emperors Go-Saga and Kameyama built a detached palace on the site, and Emperor Go-Daigo lived in it.[1]
Photo by Unknown photographer (Rijksmuseum collection), CC0 1.0.

The shogun Ashikaga Takauji founded Tenryū-ji in 1339 in memory of Go-Daigo, with the Zen master Musō Soseki as its first abbot. Its estates did not raise enough to build it, so Musō and Takauji’s brother Tadayoshi sent two trading ships to China and used the profits. The temple was consecrated in 1345 and ranked first among the Five Mountains, the leading Zen temples of Kyoto.

It has burned eight times. After the fire of 1864, in the fighting before the fall of the shogunate, little stood but the meditation hall, which was moved to serve as the lecture hall. The abbot’s quarters and kitchen were rebuilt around 1900, and the work went on into the 1930s.[1][3]
A dragon on the ceiling, a Buddha older than the temple

The ceiling of the lecture hall carries a great cloud dragon, painted in 1997 by the nihonga artist Kayama Matazō for the 650th anniversary of Musō’s death; it replaced one painted in 1899. In the abbot’s quarters, a statue of Shakyamuni thought to date from the late Heian period is older than the temple itself, and it came through all eight fires unharmed.
Behind the abbot’s quarters lies Sōgen Pond, the garden that faces the hills of Arashiyama.[3]

The head shrine of Inari, set at the foot of a 233-metre mountain whose paths run under about ten thousand vermilion gates.
Some thirty thousand Inari shrines across Japan are affiliated to this one, and the whole mountain behind it is the shrine’s precinct.
Some 30,000 Inari shrines across Japan[1]
711, by the shrine’s account and the traditional calendar[1][2]
233 m, the southernmost of the 36 Higashiyama peaks[3]
About 870,000 m², most of it the mountain[4]
Not one of Kyoto’s 17 listed monuments[5]

The shrine’s own history begins with a story from the Yamashirokoku Fudoki, an early provincial record: Irogu no Hatanokimi shot at a rice cake, which turned into a swan and flew to a peak of the mountain, where rice grew. Ina means rice, and the name Inari is traced to that event.
By the same account, the deity was enshrined on the mountain’s three peaks in 711, on the first Day of the Horse of the second month. The shrine notes that the faith may be older still.[2][1]

A torii given to the shrine stands for a prayer passing from a person to the deity, in hope or in thanks. Giving them had become widespread by the start of the Edo period, which the shrine dates to 1603, and today around ten thousand line the mountain paths.
The vermilion is a pigment of mercury and red earth, used since ancient times to protect wood. The shrine reads meaning into the colour too: the word ake can mean red, dawn or light.[4][3]

There are fox statues here, one of them pictured below, but Inari is not a fox. The shrine describes foxes as the deity’s messengers, invisible like the deity itself and called byakko-san, white foxes; not the foxes that live on the mountain.[4]

Every building on and below the mountain burned in 1468, in the Ōnin War. The main shrine was rebuilt in 1499 and still stands. The main gate is said to have been paid for by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1589, after he pledged it for his mother’s recovery. The story was doubted until repairs uncovered an ink inscription dated that very year.
Climbing here has a long history of its own: the Heian court writer Sei Shōnagon recorded in The Pillow Book of how exhausting the walk up to the shrine buildings was.[3][2]

The year at Inari follows rice. Seedlings are sown in nursery beds on 12 April, planted out in the shrine’s own paddies on 10 June, harvested on 25 October and offered to the deity on 23 November. Around that cycle come the great festivals. Hatsuuma Taisai, on the first Day of the Horse in February, marks the shrine’s founding, and visits on that day have been written about since ancient times. Inari-sai, the most important festival of the year, carries the portable shrines out into the neighbourhood from the Sunday nearest 20 April until they return on 3 May.

In July, at Motomiya-sai, people from Inari shrines all over Japan come to the head shrine to give thanks, and the approach is hung with lanterns. On 8 November, at Hitaki-sai, more than 100,000 wooden prayer tablets sent by worshippers across the country are burned in the shrine’s ritual fire, and in the evening sacred music and dance are performed in a form handed down from the imperial court.[6]

/japan/kansai/kyoto/gion/: Kyoto’s best-known geiko quarter, grown up around the gate of Yasaka Shrine, and home to a festival held every July for more than a thousand years.

Gion is where Kyoto’s arts of entertainment are still a living trade, taught for years and practised nightly, and where the city’s great summer festival begins. It is also a neighbourhood people live in, which visitors are asked to respect.
Five, two of them in Gion: Gion Kōbu and Gion Higashi[1]

Yasaka Shrine, at the eastern edge of the district, gives several accounts of its own beginnings. By its records, in 656 an envoy from Korea brought the spirit of the god Susanoo here; another view dates it to a temple built in 876 by a priest from Nara.

Teahouses grew up before the shrine’s gate from the Kan’ei era of the early Edo period. In 1881 the prefectural governor split the quarter in two, and the two halves continue today as Gion Kōbu and Gion Higashi, two of the five geiko quarters, or kagai, that Kyoto has now.[4][1]

A maiko trains for five or six years in dance, the shamisen, drums and flute, song, the tea ceremony and manners before she may become a geiko, and then she must stand on her own, without the lodging house that supported her as a maiko. Geiko divide into dancers, the tachikata, and musicians, the jikata; Gion Kōbu still keeps the two roles apart and now takes women who want to train as musicians from the start.

The foundation that supports the five quarters asks visitors not to photograph geiko and maiko, not to block the narrow streets, shout or drop litter, and not to step onto private property. This page follows the same rule: none of its photographs is of a geiko or maiko.[5][1]

The Gion Matsuri began in 869, when an epidemic swept the capital. People set up 66 spears, one for each province, in the sacred imperial garden of Shinsen-en, and carried the shrine’s god there to calm the angry spirits blamed for the sickness. The festival still fills all of July.

On the mornings of 17 and 24 July, 34 richly decorated floats carrying musicians are hauled through the streets to purify them; on the nights of the same days, three portable shrines carry the shrine’s gods to a resting place downtown and, a week later, back home.[2]

The streets along the small Shirakawa river at Gion Shinbashi were selected in 1976 as a nationally protected district of traditional buildings. The people who live and trade there write that they see it as the one place where the air of Gion can still be felt, and that the customs that kept it so are thinning; they ask newcomers to help keep both.[3]

/japan/kansai/kyoto/kinkaku-ji/: A shogun’s retirement villa turned Zen temple, its pavilion covered in gold leaf above a garden pond in Kyoto’s northwest.

The Golden Pavilion is what is left of the palace from which Ashikaga Yoshimitsu ran Japan at the height of his power, and its three storeys stack three ways of building on top of one another. It burned in 1950 and was rebuilt to the same design, which is part of its story too.
Rokuon-ji (鹿苑寺), after Yoshimitsu’s posthumous name[1]
The Shōkoku-ji branch of Rinzai Zen[1][2]
About 132,000 m², of which the garden takes 92,400 m²[3]
Special Historic Site and Special Scenic Spot (the garden); World Heritage since 1994[2][1]
Wheelchair-accessible as far as the pavilion; steps after it[4]

In the 1220s the court noble Saionji Kintsune built a villa and clan temple here, at the foot of the Kitayama hills. It fell into ruin after the Kamakura government collapsed, and in 1397 the third Ashikaga shogun, Yoshimitsu, took the site over and rebuilt it as his Kitayama palace.

Yoshimitsu had handed the title of shogun to his nine-year-old son in 1394 and taken Buddhist orders the next year, but he kept power. He moved the business of government to Kitayama, received envoys of the Ming emperor there and built up a large collection of Chinese works of art, the start of what is called Kitayama culture. In 1408 Emperor Go-Komatsu came on a state visit. Yoshimitsu died that year, and his son turned the palace into a Zen temple, as his father had asked.[1][2]
Yoshimitsu Ashikaga, Unknown painter; inscription attributed to Asukai Masachika, 15th century. Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.

The pavilion is a relic hall, built to keep relics of the Buddha. Each floor is in a different style. The ground floor, Hōsui-in, follows shinden-zukuri, the palace architecture of the Heian court. The middle floor, Chōon-dō, is in the style of a samurai house of the Kamakura period. The top floor, Kukkyō-chō, is built like a Chinese Zen temple.

The upper two floors are lacquered and covered in pure gold leaf; the roof is laid with thin shingles of sawara cypress and topped by a phoenix. In Yoshimitsu’s day the ground floor held a statue of the Buddha with two attendants, the middle floor an image of Kannon, and the top floor the relics.[3][1]
Photo by Sergiy Galyonkin from Raleigh, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Most of the palace buildings were lost in the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477, but the pavilion survived, and between 1904 and 1906 it was taken apart and repaired. In 1950 a student monk of the temple set it on fire. The building burned to the ground, and a statue of Yoshimitsu inside it, a National Treasure, was lost with it. The phoenix had already been taken down and survives.

The pavilion was rebuilt to the same design in 1955, working from the records of the Meiji-period repair, and in 1987 the lacquer and gold leaf were renewed and the ceiling painting and a statue of Yoshimitsu restored. Yukio Mishima drew on the arson for his novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion.[2][5][3]

Kyōko-chi, the mirror pond, covers about 6,600 m² and holds islands of different sizes and named stones. Uphill, water drops 2.3 metres over Ryūmon Falls onto a stone set at an angle, a carp climbing the falls in the Chinese story of the carp that became a dragon.

Higher still is Sekka-tei, a small teahouse made in the Edo period, when the declining pavilion and its garden were being restored, at the request of the tea master Kanamori Sōwa for Emperor Go-Mizunoo. Its name refers to the setting sun over the pavilion, which is at its best from here. The hall of Fudō-dō keeps a stone statue of Fudō Myōō that is shown only at Setsubun and on 16 August.[3]

/japan/kansai/kyoto/kiyomizu-dera/: Photo by Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 4.0 (resized and converted to webp).
A temple halfway up Mt Otowa in Kyoto’s eastern hills, its main hall fronted by a wooden stage nearly 13 metres above the slope.
Founded in 778 and burned more than ten times, it has always been rebuilt by the people who come to it, and its stage gave Japanese an everyday phrase.
Rebuilt in 1633 with the help of shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu; a National Treasure[2]
Nearly 13 m high; about 200 m² of hinoki (Japanese cypress) boards[1][2]
130,000 m², with about thirty buildings[1]
One of the 17 Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto[3]

The temple tells its founding this way. A monk named Kenshin, practising in Nara, was told in a dream to go north. On Mt Otowa he found a clear waterfall, and the hermit Gyōei living beside it. Two years later the warrior Sakanoue no Tamuramaro came to the mountain to hunt deer, met Kenshin at the waterfall, and with his wife built a temple there.
The temple is dedicated to Kannon, the bodhisattva of great mercy and compassion; its principal image has eleven faces and forty-two arms.[1][4]

The main hall stands on a steep cliff. Its pillars and cross-rails work like scaffolding, and the frame holds so firmly that it is highly resistant to earthquakes even on that slope. The stage in front was laid with over 166 new hinoki boards in a restoration that ran twelve years from 2008.
It was built for performances offered to Kannon: court music, Noh, Kyōgen and Kabuki. “To jump off the stage of Kiyomizu” means, in Japanese, to take the plunge on a bold decision.[1]

Fire has destroyed most of the buildings more than ten times since the founding, and each time the temple’s followers paid to rebuild. The present main hall dates from 1633, rebuilt with the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu’s support.[1][2]

Kiyomizu means pure water. The temple takes its name from Otowa Waterfall below the main hall: by its own account it began over 1,250 years ago, when a priest found a pure spring welling up deep in Mount Otowa. The water has long been called golden water and life-prolonging water. Visitors catch one of its three streams in a long-handled ladle and pray for the purification of the six senses.

Okuno-in stands directly above the waterfall. It was rebuilt in 1633, at the same time as the main hall, and has a stage of its own built the same way, from which the main hall’s stage and the city behind it are seen side by side.[5]

The vermilion Niōmon, about 10 metres wide and 14 metres high, is the main entrance. It burned in a civil war in 1469, was rebuilt around 1500 and was taken apart and restored in 2003. Beyond it, the West Gate, rebuilt in 1633, faces the setting sun and has long been treated as a gateway to paradise, a place for a meditation in which the Pure Land is pictured at sunset.

The temple keeps a full year of rites. For the Thousand-day Prayer, from 14 to 16 August, it stays open until 9 at night; it holds special night viewings several times a year, including in late November for the autumn leaves, and rings its bells on New Year’s Eve.[5]

/japan/kansai/kyoto/nijo-castle/: The Tokugawa shoguns’ base in Kyoto, where their 260-year rule was staged at the start and given up at the end.

Its Ninomaru Palace is the only fortified palace complex of its kind still standing, painted inside by the Kanō school, and in its great hall in 1867 the last shogun announced he would hand power back to the emperor.
National Treasure: six connected buildings[2]
1,016 in the Ninomaru Palace, Important Cultural Properties[1]
Since 1994, with the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto[3]

Tokugawa Ieyasu, who had won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and been made shogun in 1603, completed the castle that year as his residence in Kyoto, the seat of the imperial court. When the shogun was away in Edo, samurai sent from there guarded it. In 1614 Ieyasu set out from Nijō for the siege of Osaka, which ended the Toyotomi line, and came back to it in triumph.

In 1624 the third shogun, Iemitsu, began rebuilding and enlarging the castle for a five-day visit by Emperor Go-Mizunoo in 1626, meant to show the wealth and stability of Tokugawa rule. Even the main gate was cut down to one storey for the occasion, so that no one could look down on the emperor.[1][4][5]

The Ninomaru Palace is six connected buildings in the shoin style perfected in the early Edo period, and visitors were led through it room by room. Feudal lords waited first in the Tozamurai, whose gold walls are painted with tigers meant to show the shogun’s power. The shogun received them in the Ōhiroma, the grand hall, seated in the raised upper room, believed to face south as rulers in Japan traditionally did.

Further in, the Kuro-shoin, where he met close allies and court nobles, is painted with cherry trees in full bloom; the Shiro-shoin, thought to be his private rooms, has quiet ink paintings of Chinese landscapes instead. The openwork carvings between rooms are cut differently on each face of a single piece of cypress more than 35 centimetres thick.[2]
Photo by Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert, CC BY-SA 4.0.

On 13 October 1867, with samurai mainly from the south of Japan plotting to restore power to the emperor by force, the fifteenth shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, summoned senior retainers from 40 domains to the Ōhiroma and asked their opinion. The next day he announced he would return political authority to the court, and the emperor accepted on the 15th. The castle that opened the Tokugawa age had closed it.

It became an imperial villa in 1884. Parts of a princely residence were moved into the castle’s inner compound in 1893 and 1894 to form the present Honmaru Palace, which reopened in 2024 after repairs, for the first time in 18 years. In 1915 the banquet for the Taishō Emperor’s enthronement was held here; of the buildings put up for it, only the South Gate remains.[4][1][6][5]

A covered street of about 390 metres in central Kyoto, lined with food shops, known as Kyoto’s kitchen.
It is where the city’s ingredients have been bought and sold for four hundred years, and where you can see what Kyoto actually eats.
1615, when the Edo shogunate recognised it as one of Kyoto’s three fish wholesalers[2]
A market here in the Heian period (794-1185) is estimated, not documented[2]
About 390 m from east to west, 3.3 to 5 m wide[2]
15 to 18 °C all year, called Nishiki no mizu[2]

The answer is under the street. Cold groundwater, steady at 15 to 18 °C, kept fish and fowl fresh, and each shop once had its own well, deep enough to climb down into, that served as its refrigerator. The street was also central, and close enough to the Imperial Palace for deliveries.[2]

Kyoto vegetables, freshwater fish from Lake Biwa, hamo (pike conger), guji (tilefish), yuba (the skin lifted from heated soy milk) and fu (wheat gluten), among much else. The same ingredients go to the city’s formal restaurants and into obanzai, everyday Kyoto home cooking.
At the end of the year the street fills so tightly before New Year that moving along it is an effort, and that crowd is a Kyoto tradition in itself.[2]

Itō Jakuchū (1716-1800), the Edo painter of vividly detailed plants and animals, was born here to a family of greengrocery wholesalers; a monument near the west entrance marks the site. Turnips, daikon radishes, lotus roots and squashes, a greengrocer’s stock, fill his paintings, Vegetable Nirvana among them.

Between 1771 and 1774 a dispute threatened the market’s business. Jakuchū, then head of the district, set his painting aside to settle it, and the market association calls him a key person in its survival.[2]

/japan/kansai/kyoto/ryoan-ji/: A Zen temple in Kyoto’s northwest whose walled garden of fifteen stones on raked gravel has never been explained, by its maker or anyone since.
The rock garden is Japan’s best-known dry landscape garden and one of its most argued about: no one knows who made it or what it means, and the temple itself says so.
15 stones on 75 tsubo, about 250 m², of white sand[2]
1.8 m high, clay mixed with rapeseed oil[2]
Since 1994, with the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto[3]

Hosokawa Katsumoto, deputy to the Ashikaga shoguns, founded Ryōan-ji in 1450 on a mountain villa he had received from the Tokudaiji family, and invited the Zen priest Giten Genshō to turn it into a temple. Two decades later it burned in the Ōnin War, and Katsumoto’s son Masamoto rebuilt it.

The abbot’s hall was built in 1499, and the garden is presumed to date from then. A fire in 1797 destroyed the abbot’s hall, the founder’s hall and the Buddha hall; the hall that faces the garden today was moved from one of the temple’s sub-temples. Katsumoto, his wife and son, and the founding priest are buried in the grounds.[1]
Hosokawa Masamoto, Morita Ekishin, . Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.

The garden is 75 tsubo, about 250 square metres, of raked white sand with fifteen stones of different sizes set in groups. People call it the garden of the tiger cubs crossing, or the 7-5-3 garden; others have read the stones as islands in a sea or peaks above clouds, as the character for heart, or as the five sacred peaks of China. The temple’s own position is that the maker’s intention is unknown and is left to whoever is looking.

Who made it is unknown too. It is thought to date from the Muromachi period, and the founding priest, Katsumoto, Masamoto, the painter Sōami and the tea master Kanamori Sōwa have all been proposed. The Sōami theory was believed for a long time without proof. Two names carved on the back of one of the stones may be the craftsmen’s, but that too is guesswork.[2]

The garden looks level but slopes down toward its far left corner, so that rain drains away. The wall on the right is built lower at the back than at the front, which makes the garden look deeper than it is.

The wall itself, 1.8 metres high, is made of clay mixed with rapeseed oil. It cuts the glare off the white sand and has stood up to centuries of weather. The garden floor sits about 80 centimetres above the ground outside the wall, which helps keep it firm.[2]

/japan/kansai/nara/kasuga-taisha/: A vermilion shrine in a primeval forest at the foot of sacred Mount Mikasa, hung with three thousand lanterns given by worshippers.

Founded for the gods that guarded the new capital, Kasuga Taisha is the head of some 3,000 shrines across Japan, and its rites and buildings have been renewed on the same pattern for more than twelve centuries.

By the shrine’s account, when the capital was built at Nara some 1,300 years ago, the god Takemikazuchi came from Kashima Shrine to dwell on the summit of Mount Mikasa, for the good of the country and its people. On 9 November 768, by order of Empress Shōtoku, the statesman Fujiwara no Nagate built halls at the foot of the mountain and enshrined four gods there: Takemikazuchi, Futsunushi from Katori Shrine, and Amenokoyane and Himegami from Hiraoka Shrine.[1]

The vermilion pillars, white walls and roofs of cypress bark look as they did at the founding because of Shikinen Zōtai, a ceremony held every twenty years in which the buildings are repaired and the shrine’s tools and ritual objects renewed. Services are still offered every morning and evening, and more than 2,200 festivals are held each year.

Some 3,000 lanterns have been given by worshippers. The cloister leading to the Middle Gate is lined with hanging ones, and in the hall called Fujinami-no-ya they are kept lit, so that visitors can see the shrine by their flickering light.[1][2]

The chaos of the war years undid that. Poaching cut their number to about 80 by 1946. In 1947 the deer were provisionally named a national Natural Monument, and in 1957 the designation was made final.[2]

/japan/kansai/nara/todai-ji/: The temple of the Great Buddha, built by imperial command in the eighth century and housed in the largest wooden building in the world.

Tōdai-ji was the head of a state network of temples meant to protect the whole country, and its bronze Buddha was the most ambitious undertaking of the age. Burned twice and rebuilt twice, it shows how much each era was willing to spend to keep it.
Begun 743, completed 749, dedicated 752[1]
Since 1998, with the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara[3]

The temple began as Kinshō-ji, founded in 728 for the repose of Emperor Shōmu’s son, Crown Prince Motoi. In 741 Shōmu ordered a network of official temples across the provinces, and this one became its head. In 743 he proclaimed the making of a colossal image of Vairocana, the Buddha whose light shines over everything; it was finished in 749 and dedicated in 752 with a lavish ceremony.
As head of the system, Tōdai-ji held rites for the peace of the nation and the prosperity of the people, and it trained scholar monks in Buddhist doctrine.[1]
Shōmu Ten'nō Zō Mikenji, Unknown photographer, . Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.

In 855 an earthquake threw the Buddha’s head to the ground; it was quickly restored. In 1180 Taira no Shigehira attacked the temples of Nara and more than half of Tōdai-ji, the Great Buddha Hall with it, burned. The monk Chōgen led the rebuilding: the Buddha was consecrated again in 1185 and the hall finished in 1195.

In 1567 the temple burned again in fighting between the Miyoshi and Matsunaga clans. With the country at war, the only repair possible was to cover the Buddha’s head with copper sheets. A full restoration came only in the Edo period, when the monk Kōkei gathered donations across the country: the Buddha was reconsecrated in 1692 and the present hall dedicated in 1709.[1]
Photo by TANAKA Juuyoh (田中十洋), CC BY 2.0.
Smaller than it was, and still the largest

The hall built in the eighth century and the one rebuilt in 1195 were both eleven bays wide. Kōkei’s hall had to be cut to seven bays, because only limited funds could be raised, but it keeps the original height and depth. Even so it is the largest wooden building in the world: 57 metres wide, 50.5 deep and 48.7 high.
In front of it stands a bronze octagonal lantern from the founding of the temple, its panels cast with celestial musicians and with lions running across clouds.[2]

/japan/kansai/osaka/osaka-castle/: Hideyoshi’s castle, twice destroyed and twice rebuilt, its walls and moats from the Tokugawa and its tower raised by the people of Osaka in 1931.

The castle has been at the centre of almost every turn of Japanese history since the sixteenth century: a temple fortress that held off Nobunaga, Hideyoshi’s seat, the last stand of his family, a Tokugawa stronghold, an army base, and now a park and museum paid for by the city’s own people.
The third, rebuilt in 1931 with citizens’ donations[2]
Special Historic Site; most old buildings are Important Cultural Properties[2]

The castle grew out of Ishiyama Hongan-ji, the fortified temple that fought Oda Nobunaga. Toyotomi Hideyoshi built his castle on its site, and it fell in the sieges of Osaka that began in 1614, which ended his family’s line. The Tokugawa shogunate rebuilt it, it burned in the upheaval of the Meiji Restoration, the army held it after that, and after the Second World War its grounds were laid out as a park.

The stone walls, moats and old buildings standing today, among them the Ōte gate and its turrets, all date from the Tokugawa rebuilding or later. The area is a Special Historic Site, and most of those buildings are Important Cultural Properties.[2][3]

The main tower is the third: after Hideyoshi’s and the Tokugawa’s, it was rebuilt in 1931 with money given by the people of Osaka. It has been a museum from the start, showing changing displays on Hideyoshi, the age of civil war and the castle’s history. In 1997 it was registered as a national Tangible Cultural Property, and in 2025 the city designated it a cultural property of its own.[2]

/japan/kansai/osaka/shitenno-ji/: One of Japan’s first Buddhist temples, founded in 593 by Prince Shōtoku and rebuilt in its original plan after typhoon and war.

Its layout, gate, pagoda, main hall and lecture hall in one line from south to north, is among the oldest in Japan and preserves a style from sixth- and seventh-century China and Korea. Destroyed again and again, it has been rebuilt each time to that same plan.
Over 500 National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties[1]

The Nihon Shoki, Japan’s oldest official history, tells that during the war between the Soga clan, who favoured Buddhism, and Mononobe no Moriya, Prince Shōtoku carved images of the Four Heavenly Kings and vowed that if the Soga won he would build them a temple and work for the salvation of all people. The Soga won, and in 593 he founded Shitennō-ji, the temple of the Four Heavenly Kings.

Its plan sets the Middle Gate, the five-storey pagoda, the Golden Hall and the Lecture Hall in a straight line from south to north, enclosed by a cloister. The arrangement, named after the temple, came from China and the Korean peninsula and is one of the oldest building layouts in Japan.[1]
Photo by Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert, CC BY 4.0.
Typhoon, air raid, and the same plan again

On 21 September 1934 the Muroto typhoon brought down the pagoda, tilted the Golden Hall and destroyed the gate. The pagoda was rebuilt by 1940, and then the air raid on Osaka of 13 March 1945 burned almost the whole temple. The main compound was rebuilt in 1963, faithful to the style of its Asuka-period founding, and most other buildings since.

After the war the temple left the Tendai school and founded the Wa sect, of which it is the head temple. Its grounds cover about 110,000 square metres, and its treasure hall holds more than 500 National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties.[1]

/japan/topics/land/: A long, steep, still-moving archipelago: more mountain than plain, two thirds forest, snow on one coast and typhoons on the other.
Photo by Romain Guy from San Francisco, USA, CC0 1.0.

Japan lies off the eastern edge of Eurasia, between about 20° and 45° north. Its islands run in a curve from northeast to southwest, parallel to the continent and separated from it by the Sea of Japan. Five are counted as main islands: Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and Okinawa. Honshu alone holds 231,244 of the country’s 377,980 km², six tenths of the whole.

The country is governed through 47 prefectures, and within them 1,718 municipalities plus the 23 special wards of Tokyo. Mergers promoted by law have cut the number of municipalities nearly in half since March 1999, when there were 3,232. The eight regions this site uses to group the prefectures (Hokkaido, Tōhoku, Kantō, Chūbu, Kansai, Chūgoku, Shikoku, and Kyūshū with Okinawa) are a convention, not a level of government.[1]
Area of the five main islands, km², as of January 2026 (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan, via the Statistical Handbook).

For 35 years the figure everyone used was 6,852, from a Japan Coast Guard count published in 1987. In February 2023 the Geospatial Information Authority counted again, using its digital base map of January 2022 and the same rule: naturally formed land at least 0.1 km round. It found 14,125. Nothing new had been discovered; the maps had simply become far more detailed. The country’s area and territory did not change, and the authority expects the count to keep moving with erosion, rising seas and volcanic eruptions.
The islands are spread unevenly. Nagasaki has the most, 1,479, closely followed by Hokkaido with 1,473 and Kagoshima with 1,256. Nine prefectures, most of them inland, have none at all.[2][3]
Islands per prefecture, the five with the most (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan, 2023).

Mountains and hills cover about three quarters of Japan. They are steep and cut deep by ravines, with hilly ground between them and the plains, so farms, towns and cities crowd onto the flat land that is left.
Mount Fuji, at 3,776 metres, is the highest point. The nine peaks after it are all above 3,100 metres, led by Kitadake at 3,193; Ainotake and Oku-Hotaka both reach 3,190.[1]
Photo by Raita Futo from Tokyo, Japan, CC BY 2.0.

The islands sit in the world’s newest mobile belt, a stretch of the Earth’s crust that is still being reshaped. That is why earthquakes are so frequent and active volcanoes so common: Japan counts 111, many of them inside national parks.
Some stand right beside cities, as the photographs of Sakurajima smoking above Kagoshima show.[1][4]
Photo by Jesse Allen and Robert Simmon, Public domain.

With the mountains so close to the sea, no river is long. The longest, the Shinano, is 367 km; the Tone is 322 km and the Ishikari 268 km, and no other reaches 260. Inland water, rivers and lakes together, takes up 3.6% of the country.
Lake Biwa, at 669.3 km², is about four times the size of the next largest lake, Kasumigaura (168.2 km²).[1]
The five largest lakes, km², as of January 2026 (Geospatial Information Authority of Japan, via the Statistical Handbook).
Photo by Lonely Planet Japan, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Forest and fields cover 25.34 million hectares, 67.0% of the land, and farmland another 11.6%. Between them they account for about eight tenths of the country. Homes, factories and everything else people have built stand on 5.2%.[1]
Land by use, 2020 (Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, via the Statistical Handbook).

With little flat land for rice, people in the countryside also lived off the forests close by, for fuel, building timber and food. The Japanese word for these lived-in edges of the hills is satoyama. Taken together with their villages, secondary woods, paddies, reservoirs and grassland, such areas make up about 40% of Japan.

Some species depend on that care. The endangered Asian fawnlily flowers in woods that people thin, letting spring light reach the ground; farm ponds hold dragonflies, frogs and fish; on the Aso grasslands in Kumamoto, fields are burned each early spring to keep them open. More than half the habitats of threatened species are in these areas, and the government’s biodiversity strategy counts the decline of that care as one of the crises facing Japan’s wildlife.[5][6]

Tokyo, 1991-2020 normals: the filled band runs from the mean daily low (dashed) to the mean daily high; bars are monthly precipitation, rain and snow together, on the right-hand scale. Every city uses the same scales. Year: 12.1° to 20.3°, 1,598 mm. Data: Japan Meteorological Agency, via the Statistical Handbook of Japan 2026.

Japan’s climate is temperate and maritime, but the mountain spine of Honshu splits it in two. In winter the northwest monsoon crosses the Sea of Japan and drops heavy snow on the coast facing it, while the Pacific side stays dry. In summer the southeast monsoon brings heat and humidity to the Pacific side. There are two rainy spells, one in early summer and one in autumn, and from summer into autumn typhoons arrive from the south.

Over 1991-2020 an average of 25.1 typhoons formed each year, most in August; 11.7 passed within 300 km of a weather station in Japan, and 3.0 made landfall on the four largest islands. The normals below show the split: Kanazawa, on the Sea of Japan, gets 301 mm of rain and snow in December, Tokyo 58 mm.[1][7]
Photo by Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC, Public domain.
Photo by Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC, Public domain.

From subarctic Hokkaido to the subtropical Nansei and Ogasawara islands, more than 90,000 species are known in Japan, and estimates including the undescribed run to 300,000. Cut off from the continent by sea, the islands have many of their own: about 40% of land mammals and vascular plants, 60% of reptiles and 80% of amphibians live nowhere else. The Japanese macaque is one of them; Japan is the only developed country with wild monkeys.

The seas around hold 50 of the world’s 127 kinds of marine mammals. In Shiretoko, Steller’s sea eagles, brown bears and orcas share one peninsula. In the Ryukyu Islands, 19 of the 21 mammals found only there are on the national Red List of threatened species.[6][5]

The first national parks were designated in 1934: the Seto Inland Sea, Unzen and Kirishima in March, and Akan, Daisetsuzan, Nikkō, the Chūbu mountains and Aso in December. The 35th, Hidaka Mountains-Erimo-Tokachi in Hokkaido, was added in June 2024 and is now the largest, at 245,668 hectares of land. Hokkaido has seven; only five prefectures have none.

Five natural areas are on UNESCO’s World Heritage list: Shirakami-Sanchi and Yakushima since 1993, Shiretoko since 2005, the Ogasawara Islands since 2011, and since 2021 Amami-Ōshima, Tokunoshima, the north of Okinawa Island and Iriomote, islands known for their many endemic and endangered animals.[8][1]

If most of the land is forest, most of the people are in cities. At the 2020 census, 66.4 million people, 52.6% of the population, lived in the three great metropolitan areas around Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya. Those areas cover 33,599 km², less than a tenth of the country, and around Tokyo the density reaches 2,804.7 people per square kilometre.[1]

Buddhism reached Japan from the continent around the sixth century and mixed with Shinto, the older local faith, for more than a thousand years, until the Meiji government ordered the two separated in the late nineteenth century.

Official counts reflect that history. At the end of 2016 the Agency for Cultural Affairs’ yearbook recorded 84.7 million Shinto and 87.7 million Buddhist adherents, 182.2 million in all, in a country of about 126 million people. Religious bodies report their own numbers and define “adherent” as they choose, and many households belong to a shrine and a temple at once. The figures describe membership rolls, not what any one person believes.[2][3]
Religious adherents reported to the Agency for Cultural Affairs at the end of 2016, against Japan’s population.

Washoku, the traditional dietary culture of Japan, is on UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage, one of 23 Japanese entries as of December 2025, alongside Noh, Bunraku, Kabuki and sake-making with koji mould.
In Kyoto, Nishiki Market is where the city’s restaurants and home cooks have bought seasonal ingredients for four centuries.[1][4]

Japanese is not the archipelago’s only language. UNESCO’s Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger lists eight endangered languages in Japan, among them Ainu, Hachijō and several Ryukyuan languages of the southern islands.

Ainu, the language of the Indigenous Ainu people of Hokkaido and the far north, is the only one rated critically endangered: its youngest speakers are grandparents, who use it partially and rarely.[5][6]
